title: Nikole Hannah-Jones Has the Wrong Answers on Schools n-reform-charter
author: Mona Charen
summary: Mona Charen praises Nikole Hannah-Jones for the courage of publicly questioning whether she harmed her daughter by keeping her in failing Brooklyn schools, and she retraces the essay's account of absent teachers, ungraded work, and a daughter who needed aggressive tutoring to catch up. Drawing on her own experience in a Newark school where she earned straight A's but learned no arithmetic, Charen says the outcome did not surprise her. She agrees that most American children receiving sub-par educations are Black, but argues that Hannah-Jones devotes scant attention to factors other than the legacy of oppression. Those factors include teachers union work rules that shield teachers from accountability, discipline policies that neglect well-behaved students, and fads like whole language. She points to lottery-admission charters such as KIPP and Success Academy as proof that schools can work in spite of that legacy.
points: Charen's own early schooling in Newark mirrored Najya's experience of high grades masking a lack of basic skills.
She identifies teachers union work rules and compliant municipal politicians as obstacles to accountability.
Laws discouraging classroom discipline, she argues, leave students who never misbehave neglected.
Whole language and new math are cited as fads that crippled generations of learners.
KIPP and Success Academy, admitting students by lottery, show high outcomes for poor Black and Hispanic students.
quotes: It requires particular courage to make oneself vulnerable when social media piranhas are always circling, ready to swarm anyone who betrays the slightest sign of weakness

What followed was a familiar tragedy of American education, but one that we have become inured to. This bright, eager little girl, who came from an upper-middle-class family with a house full of books, languished.
From kindergarten through third grade, I attended a school very like PS 307. It was in Newark, New Jersey.

I share Hannah-Jones’s passion for education reform, and I admire her for so forthrightly admitting that the evidence of her own life didn’t quite match her theories. But I cannot share her point of view.
The teachers unions often insist upon work rules that shield teachers from accountability. (During the pandemic, some unions even managed to protect teachers from having to teach.)
Hannah-Jones also fails to address inane educational fads like “whole language” that have crippled generations of students who never became competent readers.

The kids who attend the successful charter schools suffer from the same legacy of racism and discrimination as the kids in failing schools. Hannah-Jones keeps homing in on the legacy. Wouldn’t it be better to focus on what works in spite of that legacy?
